~2 eV

Key idea: Increasing brightness only increases the number of photons. It does not increase the energy of each individual photon. Only raising frequency does that.
Mostly transmitted through air. Low interaction probability at this energy.
Challenge questions:
• Does a brighter low-frequency source automatically become ionizing?
• Why can X-rays pass through soft tissue but not dense bone/metal?
• Do microwaves make food radioactive after the oven stops?

Simulation 2: Photon Impact & Ionization Threshold

Part 2 · What happens when photons hit matter?

Photon frequency / energy
 177.8 meV · Infrared
Fire Photon →
Reset Atom
Below ionization threshold
Typical ionization energy ≈ 10–15 eV
Low-energy photons (radio, microwave, IR, visible) can only heat or excite electrons temporarily. High-energy photons (UV, X-ray, gamma) can knock electrons completely free → ionization.
Misconceptions to challenge:
• Do microwaves change atomic nuclei?
• Do microwaves make food radioactive?
• Are all forms of radiation equally dangerous?
• Does a brighter low-frequency source become ionizing?

headings: 16-02 Speed of Light in Different Materials
desktop.text:
Unit 5 tabs and accordion diagrams
Lesson 1, section 1: Tabs
00-00 Transverse Waves

Transverse Waves. Particle motion is perpendicular to wave travel.

00-01 Longitudinal Waves

Longitudinal Waves. Particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel.

Lesson 1, section 1: Accordion
01-00 Crest

Crest. Crest: the highest point above equilibrium.

01-01 Trough

Trough. Trough: the lowest point below equilibrium.

01-02 Amplitude

Amplitude. Amplitude is not the crest-to-trough height.

01-03 Wavelength (λ)

Wavelength (λ). Measure between matching points in consecutive cycles.

01-04 Equilibrium position

Equilibrium position. The center line represents the undisturbed position.

Lesson 1, section 2: Tabs
02-00 Frequency

Frequency. Count cycles per second for frequency; measure seconds per cycle for period.

02-01 Period

Period. Count cycles per second for frequency; measure seconds per cycle for period.

02-02 Relationship

Relationship. Count cycles per second for frequency; measure seconds per cycle for period.

Lesson 1, section 2: Accordion
03-00 Wave Speed (v)

Wave Speed (v). Wave speed describes travel of the disturbance, not the vibration speed of a particle.

03-01 Wavelength (λ)

Wavelength (λ). Measure between matching points in consecutive cycles.

03-02 Frequency (f)

Frequency (f). Wave speed describes travel of the disturbance, not the vibration speed of a particle.

03-03 The Equation

The Equation. Wave speed describes travel of the disturbance, not the vibration speed of a particle.

Lesson 1, section 2: Tabs
04-00 Frequency Increases

Frequency Increases. For this nondispersive model, frequency and wavelength change inversely.

04-01 Frequency Decreases

Frequency Decreases. For this nondispersive model, frequency and wavelength change inversely.

04-02 Visual Prediction

Visual Prediction. For this nondispersive model, frequency and wavelength change inversely.

Lesson 1, section 3: Tabs
05-00 Medium Properties

Medium Properties. The source sets frequency; the medium determines wave speed in this model.

05-01 Frequency and Wavelength

Frequency and Wavelength. For this nondispersive model, frequency and wavelength change inversely.

05-02 Crossing a Boundary

Crossing a Boundary. The source sets frequency; the medium determines wave speed in this model.

Lesson 1, section 3: Accordion
06-00 Reflection

Reflection. A transverse pulse reflecting at a fixed end is inverted.

06-01 Transmission

Transmission. A transmitted wave enters the second medium; its speed and wavelength may change.

06-02 Partial Reflection/Transmission

Partial Reflection/Transmission. At a transparent boundary, some energy can reflect and some can transmit.

06-03 Refraction

Refraction. Light entering glass obliquely bends toward the normal because its speed decreases.

Lesson 1, section 3: Tabs
07-00 Constructive Interference

Constructive Interference. Displacements add while the waves overlap.

07-01 Destructive Interference

Destructive Interference. Equal opposite displacements cancel locally; the waves are not destroyed.

07-02 Superposition Principle

Superposition Principle. In a linear medium, pulses pass through one another and continue along their paths.

Lesson 1, section 3: Accordion
08-00 Definition

Definition. Wavefronts spread into the region beyond an opening.

08-01 Small Opening (relative to wavelength)

Small Opening (relative to wavelength). An opening comparable to wavelength produces substantial spreading.

08-02 Large Opening (relative to wavelength)

Large Opening (relative to wavelength). A much wider opening produces a narrower central spread.

08-03 Examples

Examples. Sound spreading through a doorway can reach a listener off to the side.

Lesson 2, section 1: Accordion
09-00 How Do Particles Move?

How Do Particles Move?. A longitudinal sound wave moves through the medium while particles vibrate about equilibrium.

09-01 Compressions and Rarefactions

Compressions and Rarefactions. A longitudinal sound wave moves through the medium while particles vibrate about equilibrium.

09-02 Tracking a Particle

Tracking a Particle. A longitudinal sound wave moves through the medium while particles vibrate about equilibrium.

Lesson 2, section 2: Accordion
10-00 Frequency Controls Pitch

Frequency Controls Pitch. More cycles per second correspond to higher pitch.

10-01 Amplitude Controls Loudness

Amplitude Controls Loudness. At the same frequency, larger sound-pressure amplitude usually sounds louder.

10-02 Pitch and Loudness Are Independent

Pitch and Loudness Are Independent. Frequency and amplitude can be adjusted independently.

10-03 Frequency Ranges

Frequency Ranges. The frequency scale is schematic, not linear.

10-04 Decibel Scale

Decibel Scale. Each 10 dB increase means 10 times the intensity, not 10 times perceived loudness.

Lesson 2, section 2: Accordion
11-00 Natural Frequency and Resonance

Natural Frequency and Resonance. Resonance transfers energy effectively when a periodic drive matches a natural mode.

11-01 Standing Waves

Standing Waves. These curves represent particle displacement, not pressure.

11-02 Nodes and Antinodes

Nodes and Antinodes. These curves represent particle displacement, not pressure.

11-03 Open and Closed Pipes

Open and Closed Pipes. Displacement patterns: open ends are antinodes; a closed end is a node.

Lesson 2, section 3: Accordion
12-00 Source Moving Toward Observer

Source Moving Toward Observer. Approaching source: closer wavefront spacing and higher observed frequency.

12-01 Source Moving Away from Observer

Source Moving Away from Observer. Receding source: wider spacing and lower observed frequency.

12-02 Stationary Source or Observer

Stationary Source or Observer. No relative motion through the medium gives no classical Doppler shift.

12-03 Wave Speed Stays the Same

Wave Speed Stays the Same. Wavefronts still travel at the sound speed relative to the medium.

Lesson 2, section 3: Tabs
13-00 Ahead of Source

Ahead of Source. Ahead: compressed wavefront spacing.

13-01 Behind Source

Behind Source. Behind: expanded wavefront spacing.

13-02 Beside Source

Beside Source. In the classical model, transverse emission has zero radial source velocity.

Lesson 2, section 3: Accordion
14-00 Wavefront Buildup

Wavefront Buildup. The idealized Mach 1 limit has wavefronts piling up at the forward edge.

14-01 Mach 1 and the Mach Cone

Mach 1 and the Mach Cone. A finite Mach cone forms for supersonic motion; Mach 1 is the limiting case.

14-02 Shock Wave and Sonic Boom

Shock Wave and Sonic Boom. The rapid pressure change at a passing shock is heard as a sonic boom.

14-03 Not Just Once!

Not Just Once!. The source continues producing a shock along its supersonic flight path.

Lesson 3, section 1: Accordion

Radio Waves. Radio and microwaves overlap in naming: microwaves are a subset of radio waves.

15-01 Microwaves

Microwaves. Microwaves support radar, communication, and energy transfer to matter.

15-02 Infrared

Infrared. Infrared radiation can carry energy from warm objects to a detector.

15-03 Visible Light

Visible Light. Visible light is the portion detected by human vision.

15-04 Ultraviolet

Ultraviolet. UV photons interact with matter differently from visible photons.

15-05 X-rays

X-rays. X-ray images use differences in attenuation through materials.

15-06 Gamma Rays

Gamma Rays. Gamma rays can be emitted when an excited nucleus loses energy.

Lesson 3, section 2: Accordion
16-00 Refraction

Refraction. Refraction depends on refractive index and angle of incidence, not mass density alone.

16-01 Refractive Index

Refractive Index. A larger refractive index means a lower light speed at the specified wavelength.

16-02 Speed of Light in Different Materials

Speed of Light in Different Materials. Illustrative speeds; refractive index varies with wavelength and material.

Lesson 3, section 3: Accordion
17-00 Red

Red. Illustrative wavelength within the color band; color boundaries are approximate.

17-01 Orange

Orange. Illustrative wavelength within the color band; color boundaries are approximate.

17-02 Yellow

Yellow. Illustrative wavelength within the color band; color boundaries are approximate.

17-03 Green

17-04 Blue

Blue. Illustrative wavelength within the color band; color boundaries are approximate.

17-05 Violet

Violet. Illustrative wavelength within the color band; color boundaries are approximate.

Lesson 4, section 1: Accordion
18-00 Step 1: Encoding Digital Information

Step 1: Encoding Digital Information. One simplified modulation scheme maps bits to different carrier amplitudes.

18-01 Step 2: Transmitting the Signal

Step 2: Transmitting the Signal. A transmitting antenna radiates an electromagnetic signal.

18-02 Step 3: Traveling Through Space

Step 3: Traveling Through Space. Electromagnetic waves propagate through air and vacuum.

18-03 Step 4: Receiving the Signal

Step 4: Receiving the Signal. A receiving antenna responds to the arriving electromagnetic field.

18-04 Step 5: Decoding the Information

Step 5: Decoding the Information. The receiver recovers the bit pattern from the modulated signal.

Lesson 4, section 1: Tabs
19-00 Short Wavelength, High Frequency

Short Wavelength, High Frequency. Shorter wavelength means higher carrier frequency; bandwidth and noise govern data capacity.

19-01 Long Wavelength, Low Frequency

Long Wavelength, Low Frequency. Shorter wavelength means higher carrier frequency; bandwidth and noise govern data capacity.

19-02 Choosing the Right Wave

Choosing the Right Wave. Carrier frequency alone does not set data rate or range.

Lesson 4, section 1: Accordion
20-00 Distance from Transmitter

Distance from Transmitter. Greater distance usually reduces received signal strength.

20-01 Obstacles

Obstacles. Materials can absorb and reflect a signal.

20-02 Interference

Interference. Competing signals can reduce the receiver’s ability to recover data.

20-03 Weather and Atmosphere

Weather and Atmosphere. Rain attenuation is important in some high-frequency communication bands.

Lesson 4, section 2: Tabs
21-00 Bluetooth

Bluetooth. Personal devices exchange data over a nearby wireless link.

21-01 Wi-Fi

Wi-Fi. Devices communicate with a local access point.

21-02 Cellular

Cellular. Cellular networks transfer a moving connection between coverage areas.

21-03 Satellite

Satellite. Signal travel time depends on the total path length.

Lesson 4, section 2: Accordion
22-00 Frequency and Wavelength

Frequency and Wavelength. Shorter wavelength means higher carrier frequency; bandwidth and noise govern data capacity.

22-01 Power of the Transmitter

Power of the Transmitter. More power can improve the received signal, at an energy cost.

22-02 Antenna Design

Antenna Design. Antenna direction and gain affect how energy is distributed.

22-03 Obstacles and Interference

Obstacles and Interference. Obstacles and competing signals reduce link quality in different ways.

22-04 Atmosphere and Weather

Atmosphere and Weather. Weather effects depend on the frequency band and path.

Lesson 4, section 3: Tabs
23-00 Radio Waves

Radio Waves. Radio and microwaves overlap in naming: microwaves are a subset of radio waves.

23-01 Microwaves

Microwaves. Microwaves support radar, communication, and energy transfer to matter.

23-02 Infrared

Infrared. Infrared radiation can carry energy from warm objects to a detector.

23-03 Visible Light

Visible Light. Visible light is the portion detected by human vision.

23-04 Ultraviolet

Ultraviolet. UV photons interact with matter differently from visible photons.

23-05 X-rays

X-rays. X-ray images use differences in attenuation through materials.

23-06 Gamma Rays

Gamma Rays. Gamma rays can be emitted when an excited nucleus loses energy.

Lesson 4, section 3: Accordion
24-00 Frequency & Wavelength

Frequency & Wavelength. Penetration is material- and frequency-dependent; no band passes through everything.

24-01 Energy & Interactions

Energy & Interactions. Photon energy rises with frequency; ionization depends on the photon and target.

24-02 Real-World Choices

Real-World Choices. Choose the spectral band for the physical interaction or information required.

Lesson 5, section 1: Tabs
25-00 Increasing Frequency

Increasing Frequency. E = hf: higher frequency means more energy per photon. Threshold depends on the material.

25-01 Increasing Intensity

Increasing Intensity. More photons per second can eject more electrons; maximum electron energy stays the same.

Lesson 5, section 1: Tabs
26-00 Doppler Shift

Doppler Shift. A blueshift moves spectral lines to shorter wavelengths; a redshift moves them to longer wavelengths.

26-01 Color & Mixing

Color & Mixing. Adding light combines signals; pigments and filters remove parts of the incident spectrum.

Lesson 5, section 1: Accordion
27-00 What Is Polarization?

What Is Polarization?. An ideal linear polarizer transmits the field component along its transmission axis.

27-01 Using Two Filters

Using Two Filters. For ideal polarizers, perpendicular transmission axes give zero transmitted intensity.

Lesson 5, section 2: Accordion
28-00 Alpha Decay

Alpha Decay. An alpha particle carries four nucleons and charge +2e.

28-01 Beta Decay

Beta Decay. This is beta-minus decay; the emitted electron is created in the decay.

28-02 Gamma Emission

Gamma Emission. Gamma emission changes the nuclear energy state, not the element or mass number.

Lesson 5, section 2: Tabs
29-00 Controlled Fission

Controlled Fission. A steady chain reaction averages one continuing fission per fission.

29-01 Uncontrolled Fission

Uncontrolled Fission. If more than one fission continues per event on average, the chain grows.

Lesson 5, section 2: Tabs
30-00 Fission

Fission. Fission splits a heavy nucleus and releases energy and neutrons.

30-01 Fusion

Fusion. Fusion combines light nuclei; suitable reactions release energy.

Lesson 5, section 3: Accordion
31-00 Wave Models Explain Interference

Wave Models Explain Interference. Overlapping amplitudes produce alternating bright and dark bands.

31-01 Particle Models Explain Impacts

Particle Models Explain Impacts. A photon transfers a discrete amount of energy in an individual interaction.

31-02 Nuclear/Probabilistic Models Explain Decay

Nuclear/Probabilistic Models Explain Decay. Half-life predicts an ensemble trend; the decay time of one nucleus is random.

31-03 Both Models for Some Phenomena

Both Models for Some Phenomena. Individual detection events accumulate into an interference pattern.

desktop.text:
Teacher planning report • Reviewed October 10, 2026 • Recommendations only

Unit 5: Targeted improvements

The strongest improvement is a clearer bridge from definitions and simulations to independent problem solving. Sound, lenses, and spectral shifts need that bridge most urgently.

Unit 5 already contains substantial interactive material. Keep the useful simulations and the existing oscillator worked example. Replace repeated vocabulary blocks with measured diagrams, complete numerical models, and short challenges that require students to explain their evidence.

Scope: reviewed the learner-preview text and structure of all 15 sections across the five live Rise courses; compared them with seven local application packages and selected current HTML activities. This was a curriculum and selected-source-code audit, not an exhaustive test of every accordion, answer key, device size, video, or embedded interaction. Local files are not proof that their latest versions are deployed. The honors recommendations concern local extension materials. No course content, grades, or application code was changed.

1. What to do first
Priority	Change	Why it matters
1	Add real/virtual thin-lens walkthroughs to U5L3 and harmonic/resonance walkthroughs to U5L2.	The applications require calculations and interpretation beyond the worked instruction visible in Rise.
2	Correct wave-speed, photon-energy, color, wireless-frequency, and solar-fusion statements.	These can create misconceptions that later activities reinforce.
3	Make spectral-shift calculations a required preparation step before the U5L5 application.	The current conceptual explanation does not model the application's numerical method.
4	Reuse the existing photoelectric, nuclear-decay, and half-life activities after the targeted corrections below.	These already provide stronger evidence gathering than another text-only process block.
5	Replace repeated recall checks with prediction, calculation, and explanation pairs.	Students should demonstrate transfer, not merely recognize a term or the longest answer.
2. Lesson-by-lesson changes
U5L1 • Wave properties

Keep: particle-versus-wave motion, the pulse and spring models, boundary/interference simulations, and the existing example using 40 vibrations in 30 s and a crest traveling 4.25 m in 10 s. That example genuinely models a multi-step solution.

Replace/add: replace one of the two vocabulary-matching activities with paired graphs: displacement against position and displacement against time. Have students mark amplitude, wavelength, and period, then calculate frequency and speed. Include a peak-to-peak trap and milliseconds-to-seconds conversion. Label the existing oscillator question as a prediction/pretest, or place a different-number worked example before it.

Before the boundary simulator, show one three-column comparison: same source, slower wave speed, shorter wavelength, unchanged frequency. Follow interference with a signed-displacement calculation and an animation showing both pulses continuing afterward.

Clean up: the matching directions refer to dropdowns although the reviewed interaction uses pairing controls. Replace answer-revealing names such as Transverse_Wave_Definition with meaningful image descriptions. Correct “how the changing the amplitude.” Replace the ambulance-siren introduction to boundaries with an echo, doorway diffraction, or a refracted ray.

U5L2 • Sound

Keep: Anatomy of Sound, Speed of Sound Explorer, Timbre & Tuning Studio, and the standing-wave visualization.

Replace/add: put a labeled displacement-mode diagram directly before the instrument and resonance applications. Work from the picture to the fraction of a wavelength in the tube, then to the equation. Show one open tube and one tube closed at one end, including why the latter has only odd harmonics in the ideal model. Model one resonance-table row, unit conversion, average speed, and deviation from the reference speed before students complete the full investigation.

Add a quiet, user-activated beat-matching challenge: students hear or see beats, adjust a frequency, and determine whether their first adjustment helped. Do not autoplay loud sounds. Keep numerical moving-source Doppler formulas optional unless they are assessed; strengthen the conceptual Doppler activity with line-of-sight arrows and compressed/expanded wavefronts.

Application alignment: the Perfect Instrument task asks for lengths, harmonics, temperature effects, and an impossible even-harmonic case. The Rise preparation should model those reasoning types with different numbers. Its open-versus-stopped comparison should hold target frequency constant when testing the half-length relationship.

U5L3 • Light, optics, and vision

Keep: the EM spectrum overview, frequency/wavelength/photon-energy interactive, and the real-image screen test.

Replace/add: reduce the repeated spectrum/color lists. Add an actual numerical wavelength conversion in the first section. In the lens section, replace the generic “rearrange and substitute” style of instruction with the complete paired examples in this report. Each should show a ray diagram, signs, equation, substitution, answer, and physical check. Cover the object inside the focal length and the limiting case at the focal point.

The local thin-lens application has substantial signed numerical work. Students need a compact sign-convention card and practice finding image distance, magnification, image height, and focal length before it. Introduce Snell's law calculations only where they support the intended refraction task; do not add a new assessed requirement merely because an interactive exists.

For color, use three linked panels showing the source spectrum, what the filter/object transmits or reflects, and the cone responses. Let students make yellow from red and green light, then compare it with single-wavelength yellow. Their task is to explain similar appearance without claiming the spectra are identical.

U5L4 • Wireless communication and astronomy

Keep: the familiar Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/cellular/satellite contexts and multiwavelength astronomy connection.

Replace/add: replace one repeated EM-spectrum catalog with a four-bit message demonstration: choose a bit pattern, modulate a carrier, add noise, and recover the message. Separate carrier frequency, bandwidth, signal strength, and data rate. Include a carrier-wavelength calculation and a propagation-delay estimate.

The local connection_protocol_lab.html already has four technology-selection scenarios. Extend it with competing constraints such as range, energy use, obstruction, and delay. Require students to justify a choice from the displayed data instead of selecting the obvious device pairing. Label the numbers as scenario assumptions rather than universal technology limits.

Replace the “everyday versus science/medicine” spectrum sorting: those uses overlap. Ask which detector or wavelength band would reveal a specific feature and why. A same-object visible/infrared/X-ray comparison is stronger than another seven-region flashcard set.

U5L5 • Modern physics and models

Keep: the threshold-frequency idea, individual-versus-population decay distinction, and emphasis on using evidence to select models.

Replace/add: several process blocks describe a “simulation” without presenting an experiment students can manipulate in that block. Pair or replace them with the existing photoelectric-effect.html, nuclear-decay-tracker.html, and half-life-population-lab.html. Verify that the latest versions are actually embedded.

After the photon experiment, require a claim supported by two contrasting trials. After nuclear decay, work one alpha and one beta-minus equation by conserving mass number and charge. After the half-life model, calculate both a remaining amount and an elapsed time. In the final section, insert a numerical spectral-shift example before the application; it should not be hidden in optional enrichment.

End with an evidence case: a source gives individual detector hits that gradually form interference fringes. Students choose what each observation supports and identify the limitation of a classical wave-only or classical particle-only account. Avoid implying that light physically switches between two identities.

3. Definitions and statements to repair
Location / current issue	Suggested teaching language or action
U5L1 media: lower density is linked generally to faster waves, then metal versus air is used as the example.	“Wave speed depends on the restoring forces and inertia of the medium. For a stretched string, greater tension raises speed and greater mass per length lowers it. Sound often travels faster in solids because their stiffness can outweigh their greater density.” Do not apply one density rule to every wave.
U5L1 diffraction: “greatest” spreading options include both comparable and much-smaller openings.	Use a clear comparison of an opening much wider than the wavelength with one comparable to it. Do not make “about equal” uniquely correct when a much-smaller opening is also offered without more constraints.
U5L2 sound speed explained only by particle closeness.	Include elasticity/stiffness and density, with actual material examples. Replace the ear-on-train-track example with sound through a tabletop.
U5L2 dB described as loudness; danger framed around 120 dB.	“Sound level is a logarithmic measure reported in decibels. Loudness is a perception affected by level and frequency.” Duration matters for hearing risk, including at lower levels; see NIDCD.
U5L2 open/closed tube nodes lack a quantity label.	Specify air-displacement nodes/antinodes. Pressure nodes and antinodes occur at the opposite locations. Resonance means a strong response when driving frequency is near a natural frequency; damping limits it.
U5L2 oscilloscope described as showing frequencies as peaks.	An ordinary oscilloscope trace shows signal versus time. A spectrum/FFT display shows amplitude versus frequency.
U5L3 frequency determines “how much energy the wave carries.”	“A photon's energy is E = hf. Total beam energy also depends on how many photons arrive.” Use same-color dim/bright beams and different-color equal-photon-count beams.
U5L3 converging-lens rays always meet on the other side.	State the condition do > f. For do < f, backward extensions locate an upright virtual image on the object side. Define focal length using incident parallel rays.
U5L3 perceived color assigned a single wavelength; screens create “every color.”	“Color perception depends on the light spectrum and the overlapping responses of three cone types. Different spectra can appear the same color. A display produces a limited range of colors.”
U5L4 higher carrier frequency directly means faster data or shorter range.	Distinguish carrier frequency from bandwidth and data rate. Range also depends on power, antennas, obstacles, and receiver sensitivity. Higher-frequency systems may have wider available bandwidth; their waves do not thereby travel faster.
U5L4 Wi-Fi equated with internet; Bluetooth assigned a universal short range; GPS described as two-way.	Wi-Fi is local networking that can work without internet. Bluetooth range varies by implementation (Bluetooth SIG). Ordinary GPS receivers receive satellite broadcasts and calculate position (GPS.gov).
U5L4 X-rays pass soft tissue but not bone.	Both attenuate X-rays by different amounts. Also distinguish infrared radiation from heat transfer, and say X-rays near black holes can come from surrounding hot matter.
U5L5 red light can never eject electrons; changing frequency cannot change photon number.	Name the material and its work function. A threshold depends on the material. Specify what is held constant: at fixed power, increasing photon energy decreases the number arriving per second.
U5L5 Sun process moves directly from two protons to helium.	Show a labeled simplified chain: its net result converts four hydrogen nuclei into helium-4, with other particles and energy released. Alternatively, show deuterium + tritium as a separate laboratory fusion example. See How the Sun shines.
U5L5 no spectral shift implies “staying still.”	In the simple Doppler model, no shift means no detected radial motion. Motion across the line of sight can still exist. Label v ≈ cz a low-speed approximation.
4. Worked examples to add, organized by problem type

These are original tutorial examples, intended to use different numbers from assessed application questions. Reveal one decision at a time, then give a partially completed problem and one independent transfer problem. Use read the diagram → list knowns → choose and rearrange → substitute with units → interpret/check.

1 • Read two wave graphs, then calculate

A position graph has crests at 0.20 m and 0.80 m; a time graph has consecutive crests 150 ms apart. Maximum displacement is 3 cm.

Model: λ = 0.80 − 0.20 = 0.60 m. T = 150 ms = 0.150 s. f = 1/T = 6.67 Hz. v = fλ = 4.00 m/s. A = 3 cm, while peak-to-peak displacement is 6 cm.

Transfer: double frequency while holding the medium and tension constant. Students predict half the wavelength and unchanged speed, then test. Place in U5L1 section 2.

2 • Add wave displacements

At one point, one pulse gives +3.0 cm and another gives −2.0 cm. Net displacement is +1.0 cm. If they are +3.0 cm and −3.0 cm, the point is momentarily at equilibrium; the pulses continue afterward.

Transfer: choose the overlap drawing and explain why zero displacement does not mean energy was destroyed. Place before the interference model.

3 • Sound intensity with distance

An approximately point-like source gives I = 8.0 × 10−4 W/m² at 2.0 m. Assume spreading in open space with negligible absorption/reflection.

I2 = I1(r1/r2)² = (8.0 × 10−4)(2.0/6.0)² = 8.9 × 10−5 W/m². Tripling distance gives one-ninth the intensity, not one-third. Do not claim perceived loudness is one-ninth.

4 • Open and stopped pipes at the same pitch

Use v = 340 m/s and a target fundamental of 170 Hz. Ignore end correction.

Open at both ends: L = v/(2f) = 1.00 m. Closed at one end: L = v/(4f) = 0.500 m. Draw the displacement pattern that explains each denominator.

The open pipe supports 170, 340, 510… Hz. The stopped pipe supports 170, 510, 850… Hz. Its next mode is the third harmonic, not the second. Transfer: explain why 340 Hz cannot be the second allowed mode of that stopped pipe.

5 • Resonance measurement and analysis

A stopped tube resonates in its fundamental at 500 Hz when L = 17.0 cm. L = 0.170 m, λ = 4L = 0.680 m, so v = fλ = 340 m/s.

If three speed estimates are 338, 340, and 342 m/s, their mean is 340 m/s. Relative to 343 m/s, percentage deviation is |340 − 343|/343 × 100 = 0.875%, or about 0.9%. Call this percent error/deviation from a reference, rather than symmetric percent difference.

6 • Light wavelength, frequency, and photon energy

For 500 nm light in vacuum: λ = 5.00 × 10−7 m. f = c/λ = 6.00 × 1014 Hz. If photon calculations are required, E = hf = 3.98 × 10−19 J ≈ 2.48 eV.

Check: doubling the number of these photons doubles total energy but leaves energy per photon unchanged. Teach the photon-energy calculation in U5L5 if U5L3 is intended to remain conceptual.

7 • Real image through a converging lens

Given f = +20 cm, do = +30 cm, ho = 3.0 cm. Use 1/f = 1/do + 1/di.

1/di = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so di = +60 cm. m = −di/do = −2.0. hi = mho = −6.0 cm.

Meaning: real, inverted, twice as tall, on the other side; it can be focused on a screen. Show principal rays meeting there. The equation and diagram should agree.

8 • Move the same object inside the focal length

Keep f = +20 cm, but do = +10 cm. 1/di = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20, so di = −20 cm. m = −(−20)/10 = +2.0.

Meaning: virtual, upright, twice as tall, on the object side. Actual transmitted rays diverge; dashed backward extensions meet. A screen cannot capture this virtual image. At do = f, emerging paraxial rays are parallel and no finite image distance is obtained.

Transfer: students diagnose a solution that reports a negative image distance as a calculation mistake.

9 • Refraction with an angle measured from the normal

If assessed: light enters glass (n = 1.50) from air (n ≈ 1.00) at 45.0° to the normal.

n1sinθ1 = n2sinθ2; θ2 = sin−1[(1.00/1.50)sin45.0°] = 28.1°. It bends toward the normal. The frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength decrease.

Optional extension for glass to air: θc = sin−1(1.00/1.50) = 41.8°. Total internal reflection requires the higher-to-lower-index direction and an angle above this threshold.

10 • Wireless wavelength and propagation delay

A 2.4 GHz carrier has f = 2.4 × 109 Hz and λ ≈ (3.0 × 108)/(2.4 × 109) = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm.

For a separately specified satellite link with two 35,800 km legs, the one-way ground-to-satellite-to-ground path is 71,600 km. Time ≈ 71,600/300,000 = 0.239 s. A return message along the same path takes a total of about 0.477 s, before processing delays.

Check: a higher carrier frequency alone does not shorten this travel time. This is a simplified geostationary-style path example, not a claim about all satellites or GPS.

11 • Photoelectric threshold and maximum kinetic energy

For a hypothetical surface with work function φ = 2.00 eV, a 500 nm photon has E ≈ 1240/500 = 2.48 eV. Since E > φ, emission is possible and Kmax = E − φ = 0.48 eV.

At 700 nm, E ≈ 1.77 eV < φ, so no emission occurs in this introductory single-photon model. More intensity at 700 nm does not overcome the threshold. Above threshold, greater photon flux can eject more electrons without increasing Kmax.

Use a clearly named different material or hypothetical surface for this tutorial; the local photoelectric activity uses its own work function.

12 • Spectral shift and radial speed

A known rest line at 500 nm is observed at 505 nm. z = (λobserved − λrest)/λrest = 5/500 = +0.010.

For small speeds relative to c, vr ≈ cz = 3,000 km/s, away from the observer. A second rest line at 600 nm should appear near 606 nm, showing the same fractional shift rather than the same 5 nm addition.

Transfer: a zero shift rules out a detected radial speed in this model, not all motion. At larger shifts, explicitly identify the approximation's limits.

13 • Half-life forward and backward

A radioactive isotope has a 6-hour half-life. Of an initial 80 mg of that isotope, how much remains after 18 hours?

Number of half-lives = 18/6 = 3. Remaining isotope = 80(1/2)³ = 10 mg. Reverse problem: reaching 10 mg requires three halvings, hence 18 hours.

Meaning: parent nuclei transform; the whole sample does not vanish. For a small number of nuclei, calculated remaining counts are statistical expectations, not guaranteed exact outcomes.

14 • Nuclear bookkeeping and energy

Alpha decay: 23892U → 23490Th + 42He. Check 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2.

Beta-minus: 146C → 147N + 0−1e + an electron antineutrino. Mass number stays 14; charge balances because 6 = 7 − 1. The electron is created in the decay, not removed from an orbital.

Optional quantitative energy extension: a rest-mass difference of 0.0200 u corresponds to E ≈ 0.0200 × 931.5 = 18.6 MeV. Explain conservation of total mass-energy while product rest masses can be lower.

Honors extension • Clock error becomes distance error

A timing error of 0.10 μs equals 1.0 × 10−7 s. The corresponding light-travel range error is cΔt ≈ 30 m. Keeping this simple range error below 10 m requires |Δt| < 3.34 × 10−8 s = 0.0334 μs.

Model this conversion before combining signed gravitational and motion-related clock corrections. Explain that full navigation position error also depends on satellite geometry and estimation.

5. Activities and games worth using
Activity	Student action and evidence	Build decision / placement
Wave Graph Detective	Match a position graph to a time graph and moving wave; calculate speed; repair an incorrect amplitude or wavelength label. Randomize scales so students must read axes.	Extend wave-speed-challenge.html; U5L1 after v = fλ. Existing four-round prediction structure is useful.
Tune the Resonator	Choose open/stopped ends and length to reach a target note. Predict the next allowed mode before hearing/seeing it. Include a target that the chosen harmonic cannot produce.	Reuse string_pipe_harmonics_simulation.html and Timbre & Tuning Studio.html. Create a brief tutorial challenge before the separate graded Perfect Instrument application.
Image Bench	Move an object/lens and screen to make a specified image. Unlock principal rays only after a prediction. Include real, virtual, and at-focus cases.	A focused Rise tutorial is needed. Reuse the lens application's model where appropriate, or use PhET Geometric Optics. Do not transplant graded answers into Rise.
Color Evidence Lab	Produce matching perceived colors from different spectra, then change lighting on a colored object. Explain what reaches the eye.	Reuse the local Light, Color, and Vision model after its filter-off readout fix. U5L3 section 3.
Send the Message	Transmit a bit pattern through a noisy channel, then choose a communication link that meets a stated range/power/delay budget. Report which constraint fails for an alternative.	New small modulation demonstration plus extension of connection_protocol_lab.html / wireless_communications_lab.html. U5L4.
Photon Detective	Vary wavelength and photon flux separately; use two trials to decide whether brightness or photon energy explains an observation.	Reuse photoelectric-effect.html, which already has a staged experiment and questions. U5L5 section 1.
Decay Forecast	Predict population ranges, tag one nucleus, repeat the experiment, and compare actual counts with expected counts. Balance the daughter nucleus separately.	Reuse half-life-population-lab.html and nuclear-decay-tracker.html. Correct the “halve on schedule” summary first.

Success should require reasoning: prediction before animation, a measurement or calculation, then one explanation using the result. Include a restart, keyboard controls, readable labels, a reduced-motion option, and a text alternative. Completing a click should not be presented as evidence of mastery.

6. Local issues to fix before reuse

These findings were checked in current local source or assessment text. They have not all been reproduced in the deployed Rise versions.

File / issue	Targeted correction
light-color-and-vision-lab/index.html, singleResult(): after-filter wavelength label uses the filter wavelength even when the filter is off.	Make that readout conditional on filter state. White light with no filter should be described as a spectrum/mix, consistent with the white perceived-color display and full transmission.
gps-relativity-investigation/gps_relativity_investigation.html: accepts residual below 0.2 μs alongside a 10 m specification.	0.2 μs corresponds to about 60 m of light travel. Derive the timing threshold from the stated distance budget, approximately 0.0334 μs for 10 m, using the same interval as the residual readout.
honors-relativity-timekeeping-lab/honors_relativity_buzz_questions.txt, question 7: broad fast/slow-pair prompt but narrower required pair in scoring criteria.	Either constrain the requested comparison explicitly or accept all valid examples with correct reasoning. Do not require an unstated high/low-altitude pairing.
half-life-population-lab.html, ending says 240 nuclei “halve on schedule.”	The code correctly uses independent random decay. Make the summary agree: “The expected population halves each interval; actual small samples fluctuate.” Ask for an expected count rather than promising an exact future result from one random table.
fission-fusion-energy.html: displayed fission masses 236.053 u and 235.867 u are paired with approximately 200 MeV.	The displayed difference is 0.186 u, about 173 MeV. Use mutually consistent masses and energy, and label the displayed numbers' precision. Describe the change as lower product rest mass with released energy, rather than loss of total mass-energy.
Sound-resonance application terminology and spectral-shift explanation.	Use “percent error/deviation from the reference” for |measured − reference|/reference. Explain spectral shifts as a common fractional wavelength change; absolute line spacings scale rather than remaining exactly unchanged.
7. Useful published examples and interactives

Use these as teacher models or focused student links. Adapt the method to your lesson's notation and difficulty; do not assign an entire chapter merely to fill one missing step.

OpenStax Physics 13.2: wave properties: worked examples connecting period, frequency, wavelength, and speed. Best fit for U5L1 graph-to-equation preparation.
OpenStax Physics 14.4: resonance: explicit worked examples for closed-pipe length, overtones, and beat-frequency tuning. Best match for the U5L2 calculation gap.
OpenStax Physics 16.3: lenses: ray rules, sign conventions, and numerical converging/diverging lens examples. Best match for U5L3.
OpenStax Physics 21.2: photoelectric effect: wavelength-to-photon-energy and work-function reasoning. Use after students distinguish energy per photon from total intensity.
The Physics Classroom: Waves and Sound Calculator Pad: additional problem sets for wave and standing-wave calculations. Use selectively for independent practice.
PhET Bending Light and PhET Geometric Optics: alternatives where a current local visual is insufficient. Add a prediction-and-evidence worksheet instead of leaving exploration unstructured.
8. A manageable revision sequence
Correct the misleading statements and local activity inconsistencies.
Build the U5L2 harmonic/resonance and U5L3 paired-lens walkthroughs first.
Add the U5L5 spectral calculation and U5L1 two-graph example.
Replace redundant blocks with the existing photon, decay, and color experiments.
Add the small U5L4 modulation demonstration and constrained communication challenge.
Check each application against its prerequisite example, then test each revised student path and its feedback.

Across the unit, aim for one useful definition, one labeled visual, one complete worked example where calculation is required, one supported attempt, and one new-context challenge. This strengthens the lessons without making them longer walls of text.

Evidence record: rise-review-evidence.json in this folder contains the reviewed Rise DOM snapshots. The report distinguishes observed lesson content, local source findings, and proposed additions.

mobile.text:
Teacher planning report • Reviewed October 10, 2026 • Recommendations only

Unit 5: Targeted improvements

The strongest improvement is a clearer bridge from definitions and simulations to independent problem solving. Sound, lenses, and spectral shifts need that bridge most urgently.

Unit 5 already contains substantial interactive material. Keep the useful simulations and the existing oscillator worked example. Replace repeated vocabulary blocks with measured diagrams, complete numerical models, and short challenges that require students to explain their evidence.

Scope: reviewed the learner-preview text and structure of all 15 sections across the five live Rise courses; compared them with seven local application packages and selected current HTML activities. This was a curriculum and selected-source-code audit, not an exhaustive test of every accordion, answer key, device size, video, or embedded interaction. Local files are not proof that their latest versions are deployed. The honors recommendations concern local extension materials. No course content, grades, or application code was changed.

1. What to do first
Priority	Change	Why it matters
1	Add real/virtual thin-lens walkthroughs to U5L3 and harmonic/resonance walkthroughs to U5L2.	The applications require calculations and interpretation beyond the worked instruction visible in Rise.
2	Correct wave-speed, photon-energy, color, wireless-frequency, and solar-fusion statements.	These can create misconceptions that later activities reinforce.
3	Make spectral-shift calculations a required preparation step before the U5L5 application.	The current conceptual explanation does not model the application's numerical method.
4	Reuse the existing photoelectric, nuclear-decay, and half-life activities after the targeted corrections below.	These already provide stronger evidence gathering than another text-only process block.
5	Replace repeated recall checks with prediction, calculation, and explanation pairs.	Students should demonstrate transfer, not merely recognize a term or the longest answer.
2. Lesson-by-lesson changes
U5L1 • Wave properties

Keep: particle-versus-wave motion, the pulse and spring models, boundary/interference simulations, and the existing example using 40 vibrations in 30 s and a crest traveling 4.25 m in 10 s. That example genuinely models a multi-step solution.

Replace/add: replace one of the two vocabulary-matching activities with paired graphs: displacement against position and displacement against time. Have students mark amplitude, wavelength, and period, then calculate frequency and speed. Include a peak-to-peak trap and milliseconds-to-seconds conversion. Label the existing oscillator question as a prediction/pretest, or place a different-number worked example before it.

Before the boundary simulator, show one three-column comparison: same source, slower wave speed, shorter wavelength, unchanged frequency. Follow interference with a signed-displacement calculation and an animation showing both pulses continuing afterward.

Clean up: the matching directions refer to dropdowns although the reviewed interaction uses pairing controls. Replace answer-revealing names such as Transverse_Wave_Definition with meaningful image descriptions. Correct “how the changing the amplitude.” Replace the ambulance-siren introduction to boundaries with an echo, doorway diffraction, or a refracted ray.

U5L2 • Sound

Keep: Anatomy of Sound, Speed of Sound Explorer, Timbre & Tuning Studio, and the standing-wave visualization.

Replace/add: put a labeled displacement-mode diagram directly before the instrument and resonance applications. Work from the picture to the fraction of a wavelength in the tube, then to the equation. Show one open tube and one tube closed at one end, including why the latter has only odd harmonics in the ideal model. Model one resonance-table row, unit conversion, average speed, and deviation from the reference speed before students complete the full investigation.

Add a quiet, user-activated beat-matching challenge: students hear or see beats, adjust a frequency, and determine whether their first adjustment helped. Do not autoplay loud sounds. Keep numerical moving-source Doppler formulas optional unless they are assessed; strengthen the conceptual Doppler activity with line-of-sight arrows and compressed/expanded wavefronts.

Application alignment: the Perfect Instrument task asks for lengths, harmonics, temperature effects, and an impossible even-harmonic case. The Rise preparation should model those reasoning types with different numbers. Its open-versus-stopped comparison should hold target frequency constant when testing the half-length relationship.

U5L3 • Light, optics, and vision

Keep: the EM spectrum overview, frequency/wavelength/photon-energy interactive, and the real-image screen test.

Replace/add: reduce the repeated spectrum/color lists. Add an actual numerical wavelength conversion in the first section. In the lens section, replace the generic “rearrange and substitute” style of instruction with the complete paired examples in this report. Each should show a ray diagram, signs, equation, substitution, answer, and physical check. Cover the object inside the focal length and the limiting case at the focal point.

The local thin-lens application has substantial signed numerical work. Students need a compact sign-convention card and practice finding image distance, magnification, image height, and focal length before it. Introduce Snell's law calculations only where they support the intended refraction task; do not add a new assessed requirement merely because an interactive exists.

For color, use three linked panels showing the source spectrum, what the filter/object transmits or reflects, and the cone responses. Let students make yellow from red and green light, then compare it with single-wavelength yellow. Their task is to explain similar appearance without claiming the spectra are identical.

U5L4 • Wireless communication and astronomy

Keep: the familiar Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/cellular/satellite contexts and multiwavelength astronomy connection.

Replace/add: replace one repeated EM-spectrum catalog with a four-bit message demonstration: choose a bit pattern, modulate a carrier, add noise, and recover the message. Separate carrier frequency, bandwidth, signal strength, and data rate. Include a carrier-wavelength calculation and a propagation-delay estimate.

The local connection_protocol_lab.html already has four technology-selection scenarios. Extend it with competing constraints such as range, energy use, obstruction, and delay. Require students to justify a choice from the displayed data instead of selecting the obvious device pairing. Label the numbers as scenario assumptions rather than universal technology limits.

Replace the “everyday versus science/medicine” spectrum sorting: those uses overlap. Ask which detector or wavelength band would reveal a specific feature and why. A same-object visible/infrared/X-ray comparison is stronger than another seven-region flashcard set.

U5L5 • Modern physics and models

Keep: the threshold-frequency idea, individual-versus-population decay distinction, and emphasis on using evidence to select models.

Replace/add: several process blocks describe a “simulation” without presenting an experiment students can manipulate in that block. Pair or replace them with the existing photoelectric-effect.html, nuclear-decay-tracker.html, and half-life-population-lab.html. Verify that the latest versions are actually embedded.

After the photon experiment, require a claim supported by two contrasting trials. After nuclear decay, work one alpha and one beta-minus equation by conserving mass number and charge. After the half-life model, calculate both a remaining amount and an elapsed time. In the final section, insert a numerical spectral-shift example before the application; it should not be hidden in optional enrichment.

End with an evidence case: a source gives individual detector hits that gradually form interference fringes. Students choose what each observation supports and identify the limitation of a classical wave-only or classical particle-only account. Avoid implying that light physically switches between two identities.

3. Definitions and statements to repair
Location / current issue	Suggested teaching language or action
U5L1 media: lower density is linked generally to faster waves, then metal versus air is used as the example.	“Wave speed depends on the restoring forces and inertia of the medium. For a stretched string, greater tension raises speed and greater mass per length lowers it. Sound often travels faster in solids because their stiffness can outweigh their greater density.” Do not apply one density rule to every wave.
U5L1 diffraction: “greatest” spreading options include both comparable and much-smaller openings.	Use a clear comparison of an opening much wider than the wavelength with one comparable to it. Do not make “about equal” uniquely correct when a much-smaller opening is also offered without more constraints.
U5L2 sound speed explained only by particle closeness.	Include elasticity/stiffness and density, with actual material examples. Replace the ear-on-train-track example with sound through a tabletop.
U5L2 dB described as loudness; danger framed around 120 dB.	“Sound level is a logarithmic measure reported in decibels. Loudness is a perception affected by level and frequency.” Duration matters for hearing risk, including at lower levels; see NIDCD.
U5L2 open/closed tube nodes lack a quantity label.	Specify air-displacement nodes/antinodes. Pressure nodes and antinodes occur at the opposite locations. Resonance means a strong response when driving frequency is near a natural frequency; damping limits it.
U5L2 oscilloscope described as showing frequencies as peaks.	An ordinary oscilloscope trace shows signal versus time. A spectrum/FFT display shows amplitude versus frequency.
U5L3 frequency determines “how much energy the wave carries.”	“A photon's energy is E = hf. Total beam energy also depends on how many photons arrive.” Use same-color dim/bright beams and different-color equal-photon-count beams.
U5L3 converging-lens rays always meet on the other side.	State the condition do > f. For do < f, backward extensions locate an upright virtual image on the object side. Define focal length using incident parallel rays.
U5L3 perceived color assigned a single wavelength; screens create “every color.”	“Color perception depends on the light spectrum and the overlapping responses of three cone types. Different spectra can appear the same color. A display produces a limited range of colors.”
U5L4 higher carrier frequency directly means faster data or shorter range.	Distinguish carrier frequency from bandwidth and data rate. Range also depends on power, antennas, obstacles, and receiver sensitivity. Higher-frequency systems may have wider available bandwidth; their waves do not thereby travel faster.
U5L4 Wi-Fi equated with internet; Bluetooth assigned a universal short range; GPS described as two-way.	Wi-Fi is local networking that can work without internet. Bluetooth range varies by implementation (Bluetooth SIG). Ordinary GPS receivers receive satellite broadcasts and calculate position (GPS.gov).
U5L4 X-rays pass soft tissue but not bone.	Both attenuate X-rays by different amounts. Also distinguish infrared radiation from heat transfer, and say X-rays near black holes can come from surrounding hot matter.

U5L5 Sun process moves directly from two protons to helium.	Show a labeled simplified chain: its net result converts four hydrogen nuclei into helium-4, with other particles and energy released. Alternatively, show deuterium + tritium as a separate laboratory fusion example. See How the Sun shines.

A 2.4 GHz carrier has f = 2.4 × 109 Hz and λ ≈ (3.0 × 108)/(2.4 × 109) = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm.

For a separately specified satellite link with two 35,800 km legs, the one-way ground-to-satellite-to-ground path is 71,600 km. Time ≈ 71,600/300,000 = 0.239 s. A return message along the same path takes a total of about 0.477 s, before processing delays.

Check: a higher carrier frequency alone does not shorten this travel time. This is a simplified geostationary-style path example, not a claim about all satellites or GPS.

11 • Photoelectric threshold and maximum kinetic energy

For a hypothetical surface with work function φ = 2.00 eV, a 500 nm photon has E ≈ 1240/500 = 2.48 eV. Since E > φ, emission is possible and Kmax = E − φ = 0.48 eV.

At 700 nm, E ≈ 1.77 eV < φ, so no emission occurs in this introductory single-photon model. More intensity at 700 nm does not overcome the threshold. Above threshold, greater photon flux can eject more electrons without increasing Kmax.

Use a clearly named different material or hypothetical surface for this tutorial; the local photoelectric activity uses its own work function.

12 • Spectral shift and radial speed

A known rest line at 500 nm is observed at 505 nm. z = (λobserved − λrest)/λrest = 5/500 = +0.010.

For small speeds relative to c, vr ≈ cz = 3,000 km/s, away from the observer. A second rest line at 600 nm should appear near 606 nm, showing the same fractional shift rather than the same 5 nm addition.

Transfer: a zero shift rules out a detected radial speed in this model, not all motion. At larger shifts, explicitly identify the approximation's limits.

13 • Half-life forward and backward

A radioactive isotope has a 6-hour half-life. Of an initial 80 mg of that isotope, how much remains after 18 hours?

Number of half-lives = 18/6 = 3. Remaining isotope = 80(1/2)³ = 10 mg. Reverse problem: reaching 10 mg requires three halvings, hence 18 hours.

Meaning: parent nuclei transform; the whole sample does not vanish. For a small number of nuclei, calculated remaining counts are statistical expectations, not guaranteed exact outcomes.

14 • Nuclear bookkeeping and energy

Alpha decay: 23892U → 23490Th + 42He. Check 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2.

Beta-minus: 146C → 147N + 0−1e + an electron antineutrino. Mass number stays 14; charge balances because 6 = 7 − 1. The electron is created in the decay, not removed from an orbital.

Optional quantitative energy extension: a rest-mass difference of 0.0200 u corresponds to E ≈ 0.0200 × 931.5 = 18.6 MeV. Explain conservation of total mass-energy while product rest masses can be lower.

Honors extension • Clock error becomes distance error

A timing error of 0.10 μs equals 1.0 × 10−7 s. The corresponding light-travel range error is cΔt ≈ 30 m. Keeping this simple range error below 10 m requires |Δt| < 3.34 × 10−8 s = 0.0334 μs.

Model this conversion before combining signed gravitational and motion-related clock corrections. Explain that full navigation position error also depends on satellite geometry and estimation.

5. Activities and games worth using
Activity	Student action and evidence	Build decision / placement
Wave Graph Detective	Match a position graph to a time graph and moving wave; calculate speed; repair an incorrect amplitude or wavelength label. Randomize scales so students must read axes.	Extend wave-speed-challenge.html; U5L1 after v = fλ. Existing four-round prediction structure is useful.
Tune the Resonator	Choose open/stopped ends and length to reach a target note. Predict the next allowed mode before hearing/seeing it. Include a target that the chosen harmonic cannot produce.	Reuse string_pipe_harmonics_simulation.html and Timbre & Tuning Studio.html. Create a brief tutorial challenge before the separate graded Perfect Instrument application.
Image Bench	Move an object/lens and screen to make a specified image. Unlock principal rays only after a prediction. Include real, virtual, and at-focus cases.	A focused Rise tutorial is needed. Reuse the lens application's model where appropriate, or use PhET Geometric Optics. Do not transplant graded answers into Rise.
Color Evidence Lab	Produce matching perceived colors from different spectra, then change lighting on a colored object. Explain what reaches the eye.	Reuse the local Light, Color, and Vision model after its filter-off readout fix. U5L3 section 3.
Send the Message	Transmit a bit pattern through a noisy channel, then choose a communication link that meets a stated range/power/delay budget. Report which constraint fails for an alternative.	New small modulation demonstration plus extension of connection_protocol_lab.html / wireless_communications_lab.html. U5L4.
Photon Detective	Vary wavelength and photon flux separately; use two trials to decide whether brightness or photon energy explains an observation.	Reuse photoelectric-effect.html, which already has a staged experiment and questions. U5L5 section 1.
Decay Forecast	Predict population ranges, tag one nucleus, repeat the experiment, and compare actual counts with expected counts. Balance the daughter nucleus separately.	Reuse half-life-population-lab.html and nuclear-decay-tracker.html. Correct the “halve on schedule” summary first.

Success should require reasoning: prediction before animation, a measurement or calculation, then one explanation using the result. Include a restart, keyboard controls, readable labels, a reduced-motion option, and a text alternative. Completing a click should not be presented as evidence of mastery.

6. Local issues to fix before reuse

These findings were checked in current local source or assessment text. They have not all been reproduced in the deployed Rise versions.

File / issue	Targeted correction
light-color-and-vision-lab/index.html, singleResult(): after-filter wavelength label uses the filter wavelength even when the filter is off.	Make that readout conditional on filter state. White light with no filter should be described as a spectrum/mix, consistent with the white perceived-color display and full transmission.
gps-relativity-investigation/gps_relativity_investigation.html: accepts residual below 0.2 μs alongside a 10 m specification.	0.2 μs corresponds to about 60 m of light travel. Derive the timing threshold from the stated distance budget, approximately 0.0334 μs for 10 m, using the same interval as the residual readout.
honors-relativity-timekeeping-lab/honors_relativity_buzz_questions.txt, question 7: broad fast/slow-pair prompt but narrower required pair in scoring criteria.	Either constrain the requested comparison explicitly or accept all valid examples with correct reasoning. Do not require an unstated high/low-altitude pairing.
half-life-population-lab.html, ending says 240 nuclei “halve on schedule.”	The code correctly uses independent random decay. Make the summary agree: “The expected population halves each interval; actual small samples fluctuate.” Ask for an expected count rather than promising an exact future result from one random table.
fission-fusion-energy.html: displayed fission masses 236.053 u and 235.867 u are paired with approximately 200 MeV.	The displayed difference is 0.186 u, about 173 MeV. Use mutually consistent masses and energy, and label the displayed numbers' precision. Describe the change as lower product rest mass with released energy, rather than loss of total mass-energy.
Sound-resonance application terminology and spectral-shift explanation.	Use “percent error/deviation from the reference” for |measured − reference|/reference. Explain spectral shifts as a common fractional wavelength change; absolute line spacings scale rather than remaining exactly unchanged.
7. Useful published examples and interactives

Use these as teacher models or focused student links. Adapt the method to your lesson's notation and difficulty; do not assign an entire chapter merely to fill one missing step.

OpenStax Physics 13.2: wave properties: worked examples connecting period, frequency, wavelength, and speed. Best fit for U5L1 graph-to-equation preparation.
OpenStax Physics 14.4: resonance: explicit worked examples for closed-pipe length, overtones, and beat-frequency tuning. Best match for the U5L2 calculation gap.
OpenStax Physics 16.3: lenses: ray rules, sign conventions, and numerical converging/diverging lens examples. Best match for U5L3.
OpenStax Physics 21.2: photoelectric effect: wavelength-to-photon-energy and work-function reasoning. Use after students distinguish energy per photon from total intensity.
The Physics Classroom: Waves and Sound Calculator Pad: additional problem sets for wave and standing-wave calculations. Use selectively for independent practice.
PhET Bending Light and PhET Geometric Optics: alternatives where a current local visual is insufficient. Add a prediction-and-evidence worksheet instead of leaving exploration unstructured.
8. A manageable revision sequence
Correct the misleading statements and local activity inconsistencies.
Build the U5L2 harmonic/resonance and U5L3 paired-lens walkthroughs first.
Add the U5L5 spectral calculation and U5L1 two-graph example.
Replace redundant blocks with the existing photon, decay, and color experiments.
Add the small U5L4 modulation demonstration and constrained communication challenge.
Check each application against its prerequisite example, then test each revised student path and its feedback.

Across the unit, aim for one useful definition, one labeled visual, one complete worked example where calculation is required, one supported attempt, and one new-context challenge. This strengthens the lessons without making them longer walls of text.

Evidence record: rise-review-evidence.json in this folder contains the reviewed Rise DOM snapshots. The report distinguishes observed lesson content, local source findings, and proposed additions.

paragraphs.text: Multiply that flight time by the speed of light and you have your distance to that satellite. Do it for four satellites at once and only one point in space fits all four distances — that point is you.
Every GPS satellite broadcasts one thing: the exact moment it sent the signal. Your receiver compares that stamp with its own clock, and the difference is how long the signal spent in flight.
Work through all five steps. This explainer gives you the mechanisms and the vocabulary; every number you will report comes from your own measurements in Stage 2.
So a navigation system is really a clock-comparison system. Everything depends on the satellite clock and your clock agreeing about what time it is.

4 · Other places relativity shows up

GPS is the most useful test, but it is far from the only one. Question 5 onward uses these cases.

MOTION
Cosmic-ray muons

Muons created ~15 km up live only 2.2 µs at rest — long enough to travel about 660 m. Yet they reach the ground in large numbers because at 0.998c their internal clock is stretched.

γ ≈ 15.8, so the lab-frame lifetime becomes ~35 µs (~10 km of travel).

BOTH
Hafele–Keating, 1971

Four cesium clocks flew around the world on commercial jets. Eastward flights move with Earth's spin (faster in the Earth-centered frame), westward flights move against it and are actually slower than the ground.

Measured: eastward −59 ns, westward +273 ns — both matched prediction.

GRAVITY
Pound–Rebka tower, 1960

Gamma rays climbed a 22.5 m tower at Harvard. Climbing out of the gravitational well cost them energy, so they arrived redshifted — a clock at the top ticks faster than one at the bottom.

Fractional shift 2.46 × 10⁻¹⁵ — about 0.2 ns per day.

GRAVITY
White dwarf Sirius B

Sirius B packs a solar mass into an Earth-sized ball, so its surface gravity is ~350 000 g. Light leaving it is redshifted, and its surface clocks run measurably slow compared with ours.

Gravitational redshift ~ 3 × 10⁻⁴ — roughly 25 s per day.

MOTION
Storage-ring muons

At CERN, muons circulating at γ = 29.3 lived 29.3 times longer than muons at rest — time dilation confirmed to better than 0.1 % at extreme acceleration.

Rest lifetime 2.2 µs → measured 64.4 µs.

BOTH
Optical clocks on a lab bench

Modern aluminum-ion clocks are so precise that raising one by 33 cm, or moving it at 10 m/s, produces a measurable change in tick rate. Relativity is now a desktop effect, not just an astronomical one.

33 cm of height → ~4 × 10⁻¹⁷ fractional rate change.

Hafele–Keating, 1971

Four cesium clocks flew around the world on commercial jets. Eastward flights move with Earth's spin (faster in the Earth-centered frame), westward flights move against it and are actually slower than the ground.

Measured: eastward −59 ns, westward +273 ns — both matched prediction.

GRAVITY
Pound–Rebka tower, 1960

Gamma rays climbed a 22.5 m tower at Harvard. Climbing out of the gravitational well cost them energy, so they arrived redshifted — a clock at the top ticks faster than one at the bottom.

Fractional shift 2.46 × 10⁻¹⁵ — about 0.2 ns per day.

GRAVITY
White dwarf Sirius B

Sirius B packs a solar mass into an Earth-sized ball, so its surface gravity is ~350 000 g. Light leaving it is redshifted, and its surface clocks run measurably slow compared with ours.

Gravitational redshift ~ 3 × 10⁻⁴ — roughly 25 s per day.

MOTION
Storage-ring muons

At CERN, muons circulating at γ = 29.3 lived 29.3 times longer than muons at rest — time dilation confirmed to better than 0.1 % at extreme acceleration.

Rest lifetime 2.2 µs → measured 64.4 µs.

BOTH
Optical clocks on a lab bench

Modern aluminum-ion clocks are so precise that raising one by 33 cm, or moving it at 10 m/s, produces a measurable change in tick rate. Relativity is now a desktop effect, not just an astronomical one.

33 cm of height → ~4 × 10⁻¹⁷ fractional rate change.

4) Your Part 3 table records white light before and after each filter. Which statement describes what the filter does to the light?

The filter absorbs wavelengths that do not match it and transmits the matching range, so less light reaches the eye than before.

B

The filter adds its own color to the white light, so more light reaches the eye than before.

The filter converts every wavelength that strikes it into the filter's color, so the same amount of light reaches the eye.

White light is one specific wavelength near the middle of the visible spectrum.

White light contains no wavelengths at all; it is the absence of color.

Score: 2

The filter absorbed it because its wavelength did not fall in the filter's transmitted range.

B

The filter changed it into a red photon with the same energy.

C

The filter reflected it forward into the eye as red light.

D

The photon disappeared because colored filters destroy energy.

Your gray and white matches

Type: E
Score: 2
Height: 240

Always Your response is graded on reporting your own recorded RGB values for both matches and explaining what stayed the same and what changed between them. A

Partial credit: Reports both settings and notices they are related, but explains the relationship only in general terms.

No credit: Reports no recorded values, or claims gray required a different set of primaries than white.

How light reaching the eye sets perceived color

Type: E
Score: 3
Height: 260

Always Your response is graded on judging the claim, citing evidence from both of your tables, and connecting the light arriving at the eye to the color a person perceives. BusyBee scoring: Award points only in 0.5-point increments, including whole points, from 0 to the question maximum. Select a rubric-supported allowed score; never report hundredths such as 2.85/3. Do not average or percentage-scale rubric criteria into an off-grid score. A binary completion rubric still permits only 0 or full credit. Allowed scores for this question: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.
A

Full credit: Judges the claim incorrect; uses the filter table to show that light decreased rather than increased, and that the filter removed non-matching wavelengths; contrasts this with the RGB table, where combining bulbs genuinely adds light and produces brighter results such as white from all three; and closes by stating that the mixture of wavelengths arriving at the eye determines which cone types are stimulated and therefore the perceived color.

Partial credit: Judges the claim incorrect and gives evidence from one table only, or explains the filter correctly but does not connect the light reaching the eye to perceived color.

No credit: Accepts the claim, cites no data, or reverses the roles of adding and removing light.

7) This pipe is closed by water at the bottom and open at the top. Your data table contains only n = 1, 3, and 5. Which statement explains why no even harmonic appears?
A

The water surface forces a displacement node and the open rim forces an antinode, so only odd quarter-wavelength fits are possible.

B

The tuning forks used in this lab happen to produce only odd harmonics.

C

Even harmonics exist in the pipe but are too quiet for the intensity meter to detect.

D

Even harmonics would require the pipe to be longer than the apparatus allows.

Question 8
Frequency and resonant length

Buzz Question 8
MC - 2 points
Type: MC
Score: 2
8) Compare the 1st harmonic lengths you recorded for all four forks. What relationship does your data show between fork frequency and the length of the first resonant air column?
A

Higher-frequency forks resonate at shorter air columns, because a higher frequency corresponds to a shorter wavelength at a fixed wave speed.

B

Higher-frequency forks resonate at longer air columns, because higher frequencies carry more energy.

C

All four forks resonate at the same air column, because the speed of sound is constant.

D

There is no consistent relationship, because each fork was measured separately.

Question 9
Evidence for the harmonic pattern

E - 2 points

9) Choose one fork and report all three of your recorded lengths for it. Use those three numbers as evidence to describe the pattern in the resonant lengths, and explain what that pattern shows about how successive standing waves fit inside this pipe.
Always Your response is graded on reporting your own three measured lengths, describing the pattern between them, and explaining that pattern with nodes, antinodes, and quarter wavelengths. BusyBee scoring: Award points only in 0.5-point increments, including whole points, from 0 to the question maximum. Select a rubric-supported allowed score; never report hundredths such as 2.85/3. Do not average or percentage-scale rubric criteria into an off-grid score. A binary completion rubric still permits only 0 or full credit. Allowed scores for this question: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2.
A

Full credit: Reports the fork frequency and its three measured lengths; states that the 3rd and 5th lengths are about three times and five times the 1st; and explains that each successive resonance adds another half-loop while keeping a node at the water and an antinode at the rim, so the pipe holds an odd number of quarter wavelengths.

Partial credit: Reports the three lengths and notices they are roughly multiples of the first, but gives limited or vague reasoning about nodes, antinodes, or quarter wavelengths.

No credit: Reports no data, misreads the pattern, or gives reasoning unconnected to standing waves.

Question 10
Why every fork gave the same speed

E - 3 points

Height: 240
10) Your 12 trials used four different frequencies and twelve different air-column lengths, yet all 12 speeds came out close to the same value. Explain why, then account for the size of your percent difference.
Always Your response is graded on explaining why the speed did not change across four frequencies, citing your own speed values, and accounting for your percent difference. BusyBee scoring: Award points only in 0.5-point increments, including whole points, from 0 to the question maximum. Select a rubric-supported allowed score; never report hundredths such as 2.85/3. Do not average or percentage-scale rubric criteria into an off-grid score. A binary completion rubric still permits only 0 or full credit. Allowed scores for this question: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.
A

Full credit: Explains that wave speed is a property of the medium - set by the air and its temperature - not by the source, so changing the fork changes frequency and wavelength together in a way that leaves v = f(lambda) unchanged; cites the near-constant speeds or the average from the data table as evidence; and attributes the percent difference to measurement precision in locating each intensity peak rather than to a real change in the speed of sound.

Partial credit: Correctly states that the speed depends on the medium and cites some data, but does not account for the percent difference or confuses precision with a physical change.

No credit: Claims the speed depends on frequency, claims the differences prove the speed changed, or cites no data.
